events.title: Augustus campaigns in Cantabria and convalesces at Tarraco
events.summary: Augustus took personal command against the Cantabri in 26 BC, operating from Segisama, but fell ill and withdrew to Tarraco, where he spent the winter of 26/25 and entered his eighth and ninth consulships.
events.detail: Augustus set out from Rome in 27 BC, held a census at Narbo, and in 26 opened the campaign from a base at Segisama (Sasamon) with a three-pronged advance into the Cantabrian mountains. Illness, apparently a recurrence of the complaint that nearly killed him in 23, forced him back to Tarraco, and the fighting was left to his legates Gaius Antistius Vetus and Gaius Furnius. At Tarraco he took up his consulship of 25 BC, and Orosius (6.21.19) places here the arrival of embassies from India and Scythia. Tarraco later dedicated an altar to him, on which a palm tree famously sprouted (Quintilian 6.3.77). He closed the temple of Janus on his return in 25 BC, although the war resumed almost at once.
events.debate: The Cantabrian narrative depends on Florus and Orosius, both drawing on Livy, and the three-column plan is a reconstruction.

events.title: Janus closed for the second time under Augustus
events.summary: After the supposed end of the Cantabrian war Augustus closed the doors of Janus Geminus in 25 BC, the second of the three closings of his reign (29 BC, 25 BC and a third of uncertain date).
events.detail: Res Gestae 13 boasts that Janus, closed only twice before his birth (under Numa and in 235 BC after the First Punic War), was shut three times while Augustus was princeps. The closing of 25 BC was premature: the Cantabri and Astures rose again almost immediately. The third closing is undated; Orosius puts it in 2 BC to coincide with the birth of Christ, a theological construction rather than evidence, and modern guesses range between 13 BC and 1 BC.
events.debate: Date of the third closing is unknown.

events.title: Marriage of Julia and Marcellus
events.summary: Augustus married his only child Julia, aged fourteen, to his nephew Marcus Claudius Marcellus in 25 BC, while he himself was still in Spain; Agrippa presided in his stead.
events.detail: The match marked Marcellus as Augustus's intended successor in the eyes of contemporaries, and Velleius (2.93) and Dio (53.31-32) report Agrippa's resentment, which some ancient writers tied to his departure to the East in 23. Marcellus received the aedileship of 23 BC early and gave lavish games, but died that autumn at Baiae. The widowed Julia was then married to Agrippa (21 BC).

events.title: Juba II made king of Mauretania
events.summary: In 25 BC Augustus gave the vacant kingdom of Mauretania, together with parts of Gaetulia, to Juba II, son of the Juba who died at Thapsus, and married him to Cleopatra Selene, daughter of Antony and Cleopatra.
events.detail: Mauretania had been without a king since Bocchus II died in 33 BC and had been administered through Roman agents; Augustus had also planted twelve veteran colonies there (Iulia Constantia Zilil, Banasa, Babba and others) which remained outside the king's jurisdiction. Juba, raised in Rome in Octavia's household and a prolific Greek author (on Libya, Arabia, the theatre, painting), turned Iol into Caesarea with a theatre, amphitheatre and Hellenistic court culture; the royal purple-dye works on the Iles Purpuraires off Mogador date from his reign. The kingdom remained a client state until his son Ptolemy was killed by Caligula in AD 40.

events.title: Livy begins Ab Urbe Condita
events.summary: Between about 27 and 25 BC Livy of Patavium published the first pentad of his 142-book history of Rome from the foundation, which he went on writing until his death in AD 17.
events.detail: The date rests on the preface's gloomy mention of a time when "we can endure neither our vices nor their remedies", on Book 1.19.3, which mentions the closing of Janus after Actium and calls Octavian Augustus (so after January 27 BC) but not the closing of 25 BC, and on an aside in 4.20 recording Augustus's personal testimony about the linen corselet of Cossus. Livy reached the death of Drusus in 9 BC in Book 142. Augustus jokingly called him a Pompeian (Tacitus, Annals 4.34), and he encouraged the young Claudius to write history. Books 1-10 and 21-45 survive, with the Periochae and the Oxyrhynchus epitome for most of the rest.
events.debate: Some scholars date Book 1 as late as 25 or even 20 BC, or posit a second edition.

events.title: Vitruvius dedicates De Architectura to Augustus
events.summary: Around 30-22 BC the military engineer Vitruvius dedicated his ten books On Architecture to Augustus, the only complete architectural treatise to survive from antiquity.
events.detail: Vitruvius had served Caesar as an artillery engineer and owed his pension to Octavia's recommendation. The work covers town planning, materials (including pozzolana concrete), temple orders and proportions, the basilica he himself built at Fanum Fortunae, water supply, sundials and astronomy, and siege engines. Its theory of symmetria based on the proportions of the human body produced the Renaissance image of the Vitruvian man. Vitruvius praises Augustus's building programme as already under way but does not know the great monuments of the 20s and teens, which gives the approximate date.

events.title: Horace publishes Odes I-III
events.summary: In 23 BC Horace issued the three books of Carmina, 88 poems adapting Alcaeus, Sappho and other Greek lyric metres to Latin, dedicated to Maecenas.
events.detail: The collection includes the Cleopatra ode (1.37, "nunc est bibendum"), the six "Roman Odes" that open Book 3 and the closing claim to have built a monument "more lasting than bronze" (3.30). Lukewarm reception, Horace later implied, discouraged further lyric until Augustus commissioned the Carmen Saeculare for the Secular Games of 17 BC, sung by 27 boys and 27 girls on the Palatine and Capitol; Book 4 followed c. 13 BC, with odes celebrating the Alpine victories of Drusus and Tiberius. Augustus offered Horace a post as his private secretary, which he declined.

events.title: Augustus's near-fatal illness
events.summary: In 23 BC Augustus fell so ill that he handed his state papers to his consular colleague Calpurnius Piso and his signet ring to Agrippa, not to Marcellus; he was saved by the cold-water treatment of his physician Antonius Musa.
events.detail: The illness came during the political crisis of 23 (the Murena-Caepio affair) and helps explain the reconstitution of his powers that summer, when he resigned the consulship and received tribunician power and an enhanced proconsular imperium. Musa was rewarded with a statue beside Aesculapius and the equestrian rank, and physicians at Rome were exempted from taxes, but the same treatment failed to save Marcellus in the autumn. Handing the ring to Agrippa signalled that the succession was not settled on Marcellus and caused tension in the household.

events.title: Tiber floods of the Augustan age
events.summary: Cassius Dio records the Tiber flooding the low-lying city in 27 BC (read as a portent of Octavian's greatness), 23 BC and 22 BC, when the Pons Sublicius was carried away and the flood combined with plague and famine.
events.detail: Floods of the Campus Martius, Velabrum and Forum Boarium were a structural hazard of the city; later records include AD 5 (Dio 55.22), AD 12 (when the Circus was flooded and the Ludi Martiales moved to the Forum of Augustus) and AD 15. Augustus cleared the river channel of rubbish and encroaching buildings (Suetonius, Augustus 30), but a permanent board of curatores riparum et alvei Tiberis was created only under Tiberius in AD 15.

events.title: Augustus's tour of Sicily, Greece and the East
events.summary: From late 22 to 19 BC Augustus toured Sicily, Greece, Asia, Bithynia and Syria, wintering twice on Samos, reorganising cities and client kingdoms and negotiating the return of the standards from Parthia.
events.detail: In Sicily he founded colonies at Syracuse and elsewhere; in Greece he rewarded Sparta with Cythera for sheltering Livia in 40 BC and punished Athens for its support of Antony by taking Aegina and Eretria from it. In 20 BC Cyzicus lost its freedom for flogging and killing Roman citizens, as did Tyre and Sidon for civil strife. He enlarged Herod's kingdom with the territory of Zenodorus (Ulatha and Paneas), and appointed client kings in Commagene, Cilicia and Lesser Armenia. The diplomatic climax was the Parthian surrender of the Crassus and Antony standards in May 20, while Tiberius installed Tigranes III in Armenia. On Samos he received an Indian embassy whose gifts included tigers and an armless boy. He returned to Rome on 12 October 19 BC, the day honoured by the Altar of Fortuna Redux.

events.title: Marriage of Julia and Agrippa
events.summary: In 21 BC Augustus married the widowed Julia to Agrippa, who divorced Octavia's daughter Marcella to make way; the marriage produced Gaius, Lucius, Julia the Younger, Agrippina the Elder and Agrippa Postumus.
events.detail: Dio (54.6.5) has Maecenas advise Augustus that he had made Agrippa so great that he must either kill him or make him his son-in-law. Julia accompanied Agrippa to the East in 16-13 BC, where the cities gave her divine honours. The birth of Gaius (20 BC) and Lucius (17 BC) provided the heirs whom Augustus adopted in 17 BC.

events.title: Tiberius crowns Tigranes III in Armenia
events.summary: In 20 BC the 22-year-old Tiberius led an army into Armenia, where the anti-Roman king Artaxias II had been murdered by his own nobles, and set the Roman-educated Tigranes III on the throne.
events.detail: Augustus advertised the event as the conquest of Armenia (Res Gestae 27: "Armenia maiore ... cum possem facere provinciam, malui ... regnum id Tigrani ... tradere"), and coins proclaimed ARMENIA CAPTA alongside SIGNIS RECEPTIS. The arrangement collapsed within a few years and Armenia remained the chronic fault line between Rome and Parthia for the rest of the period.

events.title: Indian embassy and the self-immolation of Zarmanochegas at Athens
events.summary: An embassy from an Indian king (named Porus or Pandion in the sources) reached Augustus on Samos in 20 BC; one member, the ascetic Zarmanochegas of Bargosa, burned himself alive at Athens after being initiated into the Mysteries.
events.detail: Nicolaus of Damascus, who met the envoys at Antioch, described a letter in Greek from a king who claimed to rule six hundred kings, gifts of tigers, a large river tortoise, snakes and a boy born without arms, and the ascetic's tomb inscription at Athens: "Zarmanochegas, an Indian from Bargosa, made himself immortal according to the ancestral customs of the Indians." Res Gestae 31 lists Indian embassies as something "never before seen" at a Roman commander's court. The name may reflect sramanacarya, a Buddhist or Jain teacher, and Bargosa is Barygaza (Bharuch), the main port of the Indian Ocean trade that boomed after the annexation of Egypt.

events.title: The Aeneid published by Varius and Tucca
events.summary: Virgil died at Brundisium in September 19 BC with the Aeneid unrevised and asked for it to be burned; Augustus overruled him and had Lucius Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca publish it with minimal editing, leaving the half-lines in place.
events.detail: Virgil had been reading parts to Augustus since at least 23 BC, when Octavia reputedly fainted at the lament for Marcellus in Book 6. The ancient Life by Donatus (drawing on Suetonius) records the instruction to burn the manuscript and the editors' orders to add nothing. The poem became at once a school text: graffiti quoting its opening lines appear at Pompeii, and Virgil's epitaph ("Mantua me genuit, Calabri rapuere, tenet nunc Parthenope") was shown at his tomb near Naples. Propertius (2.34) had already hailed "something greater than the Iliad" in 26-25 BC.

events.title: Lex Julia de ambitu and sumptuary law of 18 BC
events.summary: Alongside the marriage legislation of 18 BC Augustus passed a law against electoral bribery, barring offenders from office for five years, and a sumptuary law restricting spending on banquets.
events.detail: The bribery law shows that the popular assemblies still elected magistrates in a meaningful way, and Augustus himself handed out a thousand sesterces to the members of his tribes (Fabia and Scaptia) on polling days so that they would not take money from candidates (Suetonius, Augustus 40.2). The sumptuary law set limits on the cost of dinners that were soon ignored; Tiberius in AD 22 declined to revive such measures (Tacitus, Annals 3.52-55).

events.title: Augustus adopts Gaius and Lucius
events.summary: Soon after the birth of Lucius in 17 BC Augustus adopted both of Agrippa and Julia's sons by a symbolic sale (per assem et libram), making his grandsons his own heirs as Gaius Julius Caesar and Lucius Julius Caesar.
events.detail: The adoption, performed shortly before the Secular Games, publicly settled the succession on the next generation, with Agrippa as regent figure. Coins of the moneyer Gaius Antistius Vetus (16 BC) and later Lugdunum issues showing the two boys spread their images. Their early deaths (Lucius at Massilia in AD 2, Gaius in Lycia in AD 4) forced the adoption of Tiberius.

events.title: Agrippa visits Herod and Jerusalem
events.summary: During his eastern command Agrippa visited Herod in 15 BC, saw Caesarea, Sebaste and the fortresses, and offered a hecatomb at the Temple; the next year in Ionia he confirmed the right of the Jews of Asia to send temple money to Jerusalem.
events.detail: Herod had named one wing of the Temple fortress area and a hall of his palace after Agrippa, and the visit marked the high point of their friendship. In 14 BC, after Herod accompanied Agrippa's Black Sea expedition to the Bosporus, the Jews of Ionia petitioned against local interference with their Sabbath, their exemption from military service and their temple-tax collections; Nicolaus of Damascus pleaded their case and Agrippa upheld their privileges. Josephus preserves a series of such documents, the core of the later Roman protection of diaspora communities.

events.title: Augustus in Gaul and the Licinus scandal
events.summary: After the Lollian disaster Augustus spent 16-13 BC in Gaul, organising the three Gallic provinces and the campaigns into the Alps and Germany, while the freedman procurator Licinus enriched himself by inventing a fourteen-month year for tax purposes.
events.detail: Licinus, a Gaul enslaved by Caesar and freed, collected monthly tribute and argued that December (the tenth month) made the year fourteen months long. When the Gauls complained, he showed Augustus his treasure and claimed he had amassed it to keep it out of rebel hands, and was spared; his wealth became proverbial ("Licinus' marble tomb" in the epigram). Augustus's stay produced the census and road network radiating from Lugdunum and laid the ground for the Altar of the Three Gauls (12 BC). He returned in 13 BC, when the Senate voted the Ara Pacis.

events.title: Imperial mint opened at Lugdunum
events.summary: From about 15 BC the main imperial mint for gold and silver was at Lugdunum, which struck the aurei and denarii that paid the Rhine armies; from about 10 BC it also struck the copper asses with the Altar of Lugdunum reverse.
events.detail: The Lugdunum series (IMP X, IMP XII etc. with bulls, Apollo of Actium, Diana and from 2 BC the C L CAESARES type with Gaius and Lucius) are among the commonest Augustan silver coins. Strabo (4.3.2) mentions the mint. Precious-metal coinage was moved back to Rome under Caligula or, more likely, Nero, after which Lugdunum struck mainly bronze. The ROM ET AVG altar asses circulated in huge quantities on the Rhine frontier and were widely imitated.

events.title: Augustus fixes terms of military service
events.summary: In 13 BC Augustus fixed service at 16 years for legionaries and 12 for praetorians, with a fixed cash discharge payment instead of land, ending the late-Republican scramble for veteran settlements.
events.detail: Dio (54.25.5-6) says the measure was meant to stop soldiers from being an instrument of revolution by giving them a guaranteed reward. Between 7 and 2 BC Augustus paid some 400 million sesterces in cash to discharged veterans from his own funds (Res Gestae 16). The terms proved unaffordable and were lengthened in AD 5, when a separate military treasury was planned. The professional standing army of 25-28 legions dates from these measures.

events.title: Theatre and Crypta of Balbus dedicated
events.summary: Lucius Cornelius Balbus, the last private citizen to triumph (19 BC), dedicated his stone theatre in the southern Campus Martius in 13 BC, during a Tiber flood that forced him to reach it by boat.
events.detail: It was Rome's third and smallest permanent theatre (c. 7,700 places), with a colonnaded courtyard, the Crypta Balbi, behind the stage; Pliny admired four small onyx columns there. The Crypta excavations (now a branch of the Museo Nazionale Romano) are a key sequence for the city from antiquity to the Middle Ages. Together with the theatres of Pompey and Marcellus it gave Rome some 50,000 theatre seats.

events.title: Lucius Calpurnius Piso's Thracian war
events.summary: In 13 BC the Bessi, led by Vologaeses, a priest of Dionysus, killed the Odrysian client king Rhescuporis and drove his uncle Rhoemetalces into the Chersonese; Lucius Calpurnius Piso, brought from Pamphylia, needed three campaigns (13-11 BC) to suppress them and won triumphal ornaments.
events.detail: The rebels used the Roman tactics and armament they had learned as auxiliaries. Velleius (2.98), who served in Thrace, praises Piso's handling of a war that threatened Macedonia and Asia; Antipater of Thessalonica wrote an epigram on his victory. The war shows how fragile the Thracian client kingdom remained until its annexation in AD 46.

events.title: Drusus digs the Fossa Drusiana
events.summary: In preparation for his first German campaign in 12 BC Drusus cut a canal linking the Rhine to the IJssel (Flevo lake), allowing his fleet to reach the North Sea through the territory of the friendly Frisii.
events.detail: The fleet sailed along the coast to the Ems, where it defeated the Bructeri on the river, and on to the Weser; the ships were stranded by the tide in the land of the Chauci and saved only by Frisian help. Germanicus used the canal again in AD 15 and 16. Its exact course is debated (most locate it near Arnhem/Doesburg, joining the Old IJssel). Drusus also built a mole (moles) on the Rhine that Civilis broke in AD 70.

events.title: Pyramid of Gaius Cestius
events.summary: The 36 m marble-faced pyramid tomb of Gaius Cestius Epulo, praetor and septemvir epulonum, was completed in 330 days before 12 BC, as its inscription and the naming of Agrippa among his heirs show.
events.detail: The tomb reflects the fashion for things Egyptian after the conquest of 30 BC. An inscription records that the heirs could not place costly Attalid fabrics in the tomb because of a new sumptuary law, and instead sold them to pay for bronze statues. Aurelian built it into his wall in the 270s, which preserved it; it stands beside the Porta San Paolo and the Protestant Cemetery.

events.title: Tiberius forced to marry Julia
events.summary: After Agrippa's death Augustus made Tiberius divorce Vipsania Agrippina, whom he loved and who had borne him Drusus the Younger, and marry the widowed Julia in 11 BC.
events.detail: Suetonius says that when Tiberius once saw Vipsania afterwards he followed her with tearful eyes, and guards were set so that he would not see her again. The marriage was soon unhappy; their only child died in infancy at Aquileia. Vipsania married Asinius Gallus. Tiberius's withdrawal to Rhodes in 6 BC owed something to this estrangement.

events.title: Herod inaugurates Caesarea Maritima
events.summary: In 10 or 9 BC Herod dedicated Caesarea, built over twelve years on the site of Strato's Tower, with the great artificial harbour Sebastos and a temple of Roma and Augustus facing the sea.
events.detail: The harbour moles, built with pozzolana shipped from Italy and set in wooden forms under water, enclosed some 20 acres; underwater excavation since the 1970s has confirmed Josephus's description and Italian hydraulic concrete. The city had a theatre, a hippodrome-stadium and an aqueduct, and was celebrated with quinquennial games. After AD 6 it became the residence of the Roman prefects and procurators of Judaea; the Pilate inscription was found in its theatre.

events.title: Augustus erects Egyptian obelisks in Rome; the Horologium
events.summary: In 10 BC Augustus set up two obelisks from Heliopolis, one on the spina of the Circus Maximus and one in the Campus Martius as the pointer of a huge meridian or sundial, both dedicated to the Sun "Aegypto in potestatem populi Romani redacta".
events.detail: The Campus Martius obelisk of Psammetichus II (now on Montecitorio) cast its shadow on a bronze-inlaid pavement; Pliny says the mathematician Novius Facundus designed it and that it had gone out of true by his day. Edmund Buchner's claim that it formed a giant sundial whose shadow reached the Ara Pacis on Augustus's birthday has been strongly challenged; excavation found only a meridian line with Greek labels of Domitianic date. The Circus obelisk of Ramesses II now stands in the Piazza del Popolo.
events.debate: Buchner's Horologium-Ara Pacis alignment theory versus a simple meridian (Heslin, Haselberger).

events.title: Deaths of Maecenas and Horace
events.summary: Maecenas died in 8 BC leaving his property, including the Esquiline gardens, to Augustus; Horace died fifty-nine days later and was buried beside him on the Esquiline.
events.detail: Maecenas had been Octavian's agent in Rome during the civil wars and patron of Virgil, Horace and Propertius, but his influence waned after his brother-in-law Murena's conspiracy in 23 BC. Horace had named Augustus his heir in a dying declaration because he was too weak to sign a will (Suetonius, Life of Horace). The Horti Maecenatis, with their heated swimming pool and the so-called Auditorium, became imperial property.

events.title: Census of 8 BC: 4,233,000 citizens
events.summary: Augustus, acting alone with consular power, closed the second census of his reign in 8 BC with 4,233,000 Roman citizens registered, against 4,063,000 in 28 BC and 4,937,000 in AD 14.
events.detail: The jump from about 900,000 in the last Republican census (70/69 BC) to over four million in 28 BC is the central problem of Roman demography. The "high count" view holds that the Augustan figures, like the Republican ones, counted adult males only, implying a citizen population of over ten million; the "low count" view (Brunt, Scheidel) holds that Augustus counted women and children too, implying a much smaller Italy. The figures are recorded in Res Gestae 8.
events.debate: High count (Lo Cascio) versus low count (Brunt, Scheidel) interpretation of the Augustan census figures.

events.title: Porticus of Livia dedicated
events.summary: In 7 BC Livia and Tiberius dedicated the Porticus Liviae on the Oppian, built on the site of the vast house of Vedius Pollio, which Augustus had inherited and razed as an example against luxury.
events.detail: Vedius Pollio, an equestrian friend of Augustus, was notorious for feeding slaves to his moray eels; Augustus once broke his crystal cups to save a slave. The portico enclosed a shrine of Concordia dedicated by Livia, and was a public park with vines; it appears on the Severan Marble Plan.

events.title: Herod executes his sons Alexander and Aristobulus
events.summary: After years of court intrigue Herod, with Augustus's permission and after a hearing before a council at Berytus, had his sons by the Hasmonean Mariamme strangled at Sebaste in 7 BC; in 4 BC, five days before his own death, he executed his eldest son Antipater.
events.detail: Macrobius (Saturnalia 2.4.11) attributes to Augustus the quip that it was better to be Herod's pig than his son, a Greek pun (hys/huios) that also mocks Herod's Jewish abstention from pork. The executions removed the Hasmonean bloodline from the succession and left the kingdom to the sons of Malthace and Cleopatra of Jerusalem, divided between Archelaus, Antipas and Philip in 4 BC.

events.title: Birth of Jesus of Nazareth
events.summary: Jesus was probably born a few years before the death of Herod the Great in 4 BC, conventionally c. 6-4 BC; the birth narratives of Matthew and Luke place it at Bethlehem but disagree on most details.
events.detail: Matthew sets the birth under Herod, with the magi, the star and the flight to Egypt. Luke ties it to a universal census under Augustus "when Quirinius was governing Syria", but Quirinius's provincial census of Judaea took place in AD 6, ten years after Herod's death, and no empire-wide census of the kind Luke describes is attested. Attempts to rescue Luke with an earlier governorship of Quirinius, or to identify the star with the Jupiter-Saturn conjunctions of 7 BC or a comet of 5 BC, remain speculative. The AD era itself derives from Dionysius Exiguus (AD 525), whose reckoning puts the birth after Herod's death and is generally reckoned a few years too late. Many critical scholars regard the Bethlehem setting as theological (Davidic descent) and Nazareth as the actual place of birth.
events.debate: Luke's census of Quirinius conflicts with Matthew's Herodian dating; the AD 6 census is securely attested by Josephus.

events.title: Agrippa's world map displayed in the Porticus Vipsania
events.summary: The world map compiled from Agrippa's commentaries was set up after his death in the Porticus Vipsania, completed by his sister Vipsania Polla and Augustus around 7 BC.
events.detail: Pliny the Elder cites Agrippa's measurements (in Roman miles) for dozens of provinces and seas, often critically, and says Augustus completed the portico on Agrippa's plan. The form of the map (a painted or carved orbis terrarum, perhaps oval) is unknown; it lies behind later itineraries and has been connected with the ancestry of the Peutinger Table.

events.title: Augustus's naumachia and the Aqua Alsietina
events.summary: For the dedication of the Temple of Mars Ultor in 2 BC Augustus staged a sea battle of Athenians against Persians, with 30 rams and 3,000 men besides rowers, in a basin 1,800 by 1,200 feet dug across the Tiber.
events.detail: The basin was fed by the new Aqua Alsietina, a low-quality aqueduct from Lake Alsietinus (Martignano) that Frontinus says was fit only for the naumachia and for watering gardens. The show reenacted Salamis, an allusion to Actium. Crocodiles were also killed in the Circus Flaminius flooded for the occasion (Dio 55.10.8). The naumachia survived until at least the third century, when Titus and Nero had used it for shows.

events.title: Ovid publishes the Ars Amatoria
events.summary: Around 2 BC to AD 2 Ovid issued the Ars Amatoria, a mock-didactic manual of seduction in three books, which he later named as one of the two causes ("carmen et error") of his relegation to Tomis in AD 8.
events.detail: Published in the year of Julia's disgrace and soon after the adultery laws, its jokes about married women and the Augustan monuments as pick-up venues sat ill with official morality; Ovid insisted in the Tristia that the poem was written for courtesans only. The Remedia Amoris followed. The Metamorphoses, completed by AD 8, and the unfinished Fasti were the major works of his last years in Rome. The books were removed from the public libraries after his exile.

events.title: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus crosses the Elbe
events.summary: As legate of Illyricum and then of Germany, Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus (cos. 16 BC) resettled wandering Hermunduri, crossed the Elbe unopposed some time between 7 BC and AD 1, set up an altar to Augustus on its far bank and built the causeway roads called pontes longi across the marshes between the Rhine and Ems.
events.detail: Ahenobarbus, Nero's grandfather, received triumphal ornaments; Suetonius (Nero 4) describes him as arrogant and cruel, a lover of chariot racing. His intervention in Cherusci politics, trying to restore exiled nobles, was a failure. The pontes longi were reused, and nearly cost Caecina his army, in AD 15.
events.debate: Date uncertain (Dio's text is fragmentary); placed between c. 7 BC and AD 1.

events.title: Tiberius returns from Rhodes
events.summary: With Gaius Caesar's consent and Livia's pleading, Tiberius was allowed to return from his seven-year retirement on Rhodes in AD 2, on condition that he take no part in public affairs; he lived in the Gardens of Maecenas.
events.detail: On Rhodes Tiberius had studied with the astrologer Thrasyllus, attended philosophical lectures and visited Gaius at Samos, where Gaius's companion Marcus Lollius poisoned the meeting. His tribunician power had lapsed and the people of Nemausus had thrown down his statues. Lollius's disgrace and death and then the death of Lucius at Massilia that summer cleared the way for his rehabilitation and adoption in AD 4.

events.title: Siege of Artagira; Gaius Caesar wounded
events.summary: Gaius Caesar, sent to settle Armenia, was treacherously wounded on 9 September AD 3 by Addon, commander of the fortress of Artagira, during a parley; the fort was taken after a long siege, but Gaius never recovered and died in Lycia in February AD 4.
events.detail: Gaius had installed the Median prince Ariobarzanes as king of Armenia against the pro-Parthian faction after his meeting with Phraataces on the Euphrates in AD 2. Velleius says the wound left him in body and mind unfit for service and that he asked to retire to Syria; the Fasti Cuprenses give the date of the wound. His death removed Augustus's chosen heir and led to the adoption of Tiberius.

events.title: Augustus pardons the conspirator Cinna
events.summary: Seneca and Dio tell how Augustus, on Livia's advice, pardoned Gnaeus Cornelius Cinna Magnus, Pompey's grandson, who had plotted to kill him, and made him consul the next year (AD 5).
events.detail: Seneca's De Clementia (1.9) sets the episode in Gaul when Augustus was forty (c. 16-13 BC) and has Augustus lecture Cinna for two hours; Dio (55.14-22) places it in AD 4 and gives Livia a long speech on the benefits of mercy. Cinna was indeed consul in AD 5, which favours Dio's context. Corneille turned the story into his tragedy Cinna (1641).
events.debate: Seneca and Dio differ on the date (16-13 BC or AD 4); the story may be embellished as an exemplum of clemency.

events.title: Military service extended to twenty years
events.summary: In AD 5 legionary service was raised to 20 years (with a further five sub vexillo as veterans) and praetorian service to 16, with discharge bounties of 12,000 sesterces for legionaries and 20,000 for praetorians.
events.detail: The change acknowledged that the 13 BC terms were unaffordable; it led directly to the aerarium militare of AD 6, financed by a 5% inheritance tax and a 1% sales tax. Long service without promised discharge was a main grievance of the mutinous legions of AD 14, who complained of being kept on for thirty or forty years and paid in "swamps and mountainsides" instead of land.

events.title: Lex Valeria Cornelia and the destinatio centuries
events.summary: A law of AD 5 created ten new voting centuries of senators and equestrians, named after Gaius and Lucius Caesar, whose preliminary vote (destinatio) on consular and praetorian candidates guided the full Centuriate Assembly.
events.detail: The law is known only from the Tabula Hebana (found 1947), which records the addition of five further centuries named after Germanicus in AD 19 and five after Drusus the Younger in AD 23. It shows how Augustus managed elections through the upper orders while preserving the assembly's formal role, a stage on the way to the transfer of elections to the Senate in AD 14.

events.title: Famine and unrest at Rome in AD 6
events.summary: A severe grain shortage in AD 6 led Augustus to expel gladiators, slaves for sale and most foreigners (except doctors and teachers) to beyond the hundredth milestone, double the grain dole and appoint two consulars as grain commissioners.
events.detail: Senators were allowed to leave the city and the courts were suspended. The famine coincided with the fire that led to the creation of the vigiles, the new taxes of the aerarium militare and the outbreak of the Illyrian revolt, which Dio (55.27) describes as a time of lampoons and talk of revolution; one Publius Rufus was suspected of circulating seditious pamphlets. Germanicus and his brother gave games in honour of the dead Drusus to soothe the people.

events.title: Cossus Cornelius Lentulus's Gaetulian war
events.summary: Around AD 6 the proconsul of Africa Cossus Cornelius Lentulus defeated the Gaetuli and Musulamii, who had attacked the territory of Juba II and Roman Africa, earning triumphal ornaments and the cognomen Gaetulicus for his son.
events.detail: An inscription from Lepcis Magna records the "freeing of Africa from the Gaetulian war" under Cossus. The war foreshadowed the much longer revolt of Tacfarinas, a Musulamian, from AD 17. Gaetulicus the younger, consul in 26, later commanded Upper Germany and was executed by Caligula in 39.

events.title: Tiberius's planned pincer attack on Maroboduus
events.summary: In AD 6 Tiberius prepared a two-pronged invasion of Maroboduus's Marcomannic kingdom in Bohemia, with Sentius Saturninus advancing from the Rhine through the Hercynian forest and Tiberius from Carnuntum, using twelve legions; the outbreak of the Pannonian-Dalmatian revolt forced him to abandon it within days of contact.
events.detail: Velleius (2.108-110), who served as Tiberius's officer, describes Maroboduus's army of 70,000 foot and 4,000 horse drilled in Roman fashion and his kingdom as a threat to Italy. A hasty peace recognised Maroboduus as a friend of Rome, and he stayed neutral in AD 9 after Varus's defeat. Recent finds of Roman marching camps in Moravia and Lower Austria (e.g. Musov) may relate to these or later operations.

events.title: Judas the Galilean and the census revolt
events.summary: When Quirinius registered Judaea for tribute in AD 6, Judas of Gamala (the Galilean) and the Pharisee Saddok called on Jews to refuse it, teaching that God alone was master; Josephus calls the movement a "fourth philosophy" and blames it for the later revolt.
events.detail: The High Priest Joazar persuaded most to accept the census. Judas's fate is not recorded by Josephus, but Acts 5.37 says he perished. His sons James and Simon were crucified by Tiberius Julius Alexander c. 46-48, another son (or grandson) Menahem seized Masada and led a faction in 66, and his descendant Eleazar ben Yair commanded Masada to its fall in 73/74.

events.title: Tiberius dedicates the Temple of Concord
events.summary: On 16 January AD 10 Tiberius dedicated the rebuilt Temple of Concord at the foot of the Capitol in his own name and that of his dead brother Drusus, paid for from German spoils.
events.detail: The temple, with its unusual wide cella, became a museum of Greek art: Pliny lists works by Zeuxis, Nicias, Theodorus and Sthennis, and Livia dedicated a sardonyx of Polycrates. It was a frequent meeting place of the Senate (Sejanus was condemned there in 31). Tiberius also rebuilt the Temple of Castor (dedicated AD 6) in the names of himself and Drusus, the twin dedications projecting fraternal concordia within the dynasty.

events.title: Senatus consultum Silanianum
events.summary: A decree of the Senate of AD 10 provided that if a master was murdered at home, all the slaves under the same roof were to be tortured and executed, a rule applied with full rigour in the Pedanius Secundus case of AD 61.
events.detail: The decree, named after the consul Gaius Junius Silanus, aimed to make every slave a guard over his master's life; a slave who could not have helped (being out of earshot or chained) was exempt. Its interpretation fills Digest 29.5. In AD 61, 400 slaves of the murdered urban prefect were executed after a famous debate in the Senate in which Gaius Cassius Longinus defended the custom.

events.title: Tiberius and Germanicus restore the Rhine frontier
events.summary: After the Varian disaster Tiberius took command on the Rhine (AD 10-12), raised the garrison to eight legions and made cautious incursions across the river with Germanicus, avoiding battle and taking no unnecessary risks.
events.detail: Suetonius (Tiberius 18) describes his precautions: he limited baggage, checked the loading of every wagon, slept without a tent and gave orders in writing. Dio says he crossed the Rhine but did not advance far or win a battle. The two new legions on the Rhine (XXI Rapax and V Alaudae or I Germanica moved up) brought the force to eight, the largest concentration in the empire until the 80s. Tiberius returned to Rome for his Pannonian triumph in October 12.

events.title: Augustus's last census: 4,937,000 citizens
events.summary: Augustus and Tiberius completed a census and lustrum in AD 14, registering 4,937,000 citizens, just before Augustus left Rome for the last time; a snake was seen in the Campus Martius during the closing ceremony, read later as an omen of his death.
events.detail: Augustus took a vow for the next lustrum but declined to pronounce it, as he would not live to fulfil it (Suetonius, Augustus 97). The increase of some 700,000 over 8 BC reflects manumission, grants to provincials and natural growth. This was the last regular census of citizens; Claudius (47/48) and Vespasian (73/74) revived it.

events.title: Augustus grants the ius respondendi
events.summary: According to the jurist Pomponius, Augustus was the first to give selected jurists the right to give legal opinions (responsa) "by his authority", tying private legal expertise to the princeps.
events.detail: Pomponius (Digest 1.2.2.48-50) says that before Augustus anyone confident in his learning gave opinions; Augustus wanted their authority enhanced and Tiberius gave the privilege to Masurius Sabinus, the first equestrian so honoured. How binding such responsa were on judges is unclear before Hadrian, who ruled that where licensed jurists agreed their view had the force of law. The date of Augustus's grant is unknown.
events.debate: Nature and date of the privilege are disputed; some doubt that it gave formally binding force.

events.title: The rival law schools of Labeo and Capito
events.summary: Under Augustus the jurists Marcus Antistius Labeo, a republican who refused the consulship, and Gaius Ateius Capito, a loyalist consul of AD 5, founded the two schools later called Proculians (after Proculus) and Sabinians (after Masurius Sabinus and Cassius Longinus).
events.detail: Pomponius says Labeo was innovative and confident in his own learning, Capito conservative. The schools disputed dozens of questions until the mid-second century: for instance whether a new object made from another's material (specificatio) belonged to the maker (Proculians) or the owner of the material (Sabinians), and the age of puberty. Gaius, writing c. 161, still calls the Sabinians "our teachers". Labeo wrote some 400 books; Tacitus (Annals 3.75) contrasts his incorruptible freedom with Capito's servility.

events.title: Maison Carree at Nemausus dedicated to Gaius and Lucius
events.summary: The best-preserved Roman temple anywhere, the Maison Carree at Nemausus, carried a bronze inscription (reconstructed from its nail holes in 1758) dedicating it to Gaius and Lucius Caesar as consuls designate and principes iuventutis, so c. AD 2-4.
events.detail: The temple, a hexastyle pseudoperipteral Corinthian building on a high podium, was probably begun under Agrippa's patronage c. 20-12 BC and rededicated to the dead princes. Its decoration copies the Forum of Augustus workshops. The temple survived as a consular house, stable and church, and inspired Thomas Jefferson's Virginia State Capitol. The Pont du Gard brought water to the same colony a generation later.
events.debate: The first phase may date to c. 16 BC with a dedication to Agrippa; the Gaius and Lucius inscription is the second.

events.title: Tiberius halves the sales tax; fortunes of the Augustan taxes
events.summary: In AD 17, using the new revenues of Cappadocia, Tiberius halved the 1% sales tax (centesima rerum venalium) that Augustus had imposed alongside the 5% inheritance tax to fund veteran bounties, the first direct burdens on Roman citizens in Italy since 167 BC.
events.detail: The inheritance tax was deeply resented; in AD 13 Augustus threatened a land tax instead, and the Senate accepted the 5%. Tiberius halved the sales tax to 0.5% after the annexation of Cappadocia in AD 17 and restored it in 31; Caligula abolished it in Italy in 38. Caracalla later doubled the inheritance tax to 10% and, according to Dio, extended citizenship partly to broaden its base.
